job: perfect tense of an intransitive verb, formed with be and the past participle, expressing the state reached
definition: In intransitive verbs, forming tenses of the perfect; in later use chiefly with verbs of motion such as come, go, rise, set, fall, arrive, depart, grow, etc., expressing a condition or state attained at the time of speaking, rather than the action of reaching it, e.g. ‘the sun is set’, ‘our guests are gone’, ‘Babylon is fallen’, ‘the children are all grown up’. Smith, San Francisco's Lost Landmarks, 2005).

definition: Verb: to guard, stand guard over; to keep in safety, take care of; to defend, protect (OED ward v.1, sense 1.a); to defend or protect from (1.b); to avert, keep off harm or danger (7); intransitive, to take up a position of defence, take precautions against (8, obsolete). Noun: a watchman, guard, keeper, warden (OED ward n.1, obsolete, Old English to 1473).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED ward v.1 and ward n.1): VERB sense 1.a, to guard or keep safe with a direct object, OE-LMdE: OE "Þa Englisce men þe wærdedon þære sæ." (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, MS Laud, annal 1087); ME (c1384) "Thei goynge forth, kepten, or wardiden, the sepulcre." (Wycliffite Bible, Early Version, Matthew xxvii. 66); EMdE 1597 "Then if you fight against Gods enemie, God will in iustice, ward you as his souldiers." (Shakespeare, Richard III v. v. 208); LMdE 1893 "Hope Park, a beautiful pleasance..warded by a keeper." (R. L. Stevenson, Catriona viii. 87); latest 1913 "Your wits must ward your head." (Blackwood's Magazine, December 787/1). Sense 1.b, to defend or protect from, ?c1225-1850: ?c1225 "Biseched ȝeorne god..þet he wite & wardi ow wið alle þet ou weited." Wright, Passions of Minde vi. 318); LMdE 1850 "Loxias himself will ward His holiest shrine from lawless outrage." (J. S. Blackie, trans. Aeschylus). Sense 1.d, intransitive, to keep guard, ME-LMdE: 1390 "And in this hous to loke and warde Was Minotaurus put in warde." (Gower, Confessio Amantis); 1722 "The Family..left the..Fellows warding, and watching." (Defoe, Journal of the Plague Year 63). Sense 2, to rule or act as guardian, OE-1400: OE "Nabochodonossor.. weardode wide rice." (Caedmon's Dan. 665); 1390 "tok this child into his warde, And seide he wolde him kepe and warde." (Gower, Confessio Amantis I. 345). Sense 7, to avert or keep off harm, a1586-: a1586 "While they did ward sun-beames with shady bay." (Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia); 1810 "I, only I, can ward their fate." (W. Scott, The Lady of the Lake v. 220); with off (7.b) 1759 "If then you would ward off the gripe of poverty, pretend to be a stranger to her." (O. Goldsmith, Bee). Sense 8, intransitive, to take precautions against (obsolete, 1230-1753): 1709 "To ward against the coming Blow." (M. Prior, Paulo Purganti 100); 1726 "Regard must be had..in cold Countries to ward against the bleak Northwind." (G. Leoni, trans. L. B. Alberti, Architecture I. 99); 1745 "In England, this pusillanimity is more to be warded against than in most other countries." (J. Swift). Sense 1.c, figurative, to guard a secret, 1881: "obliges me to ward a secret." (A. J. Duffield, trans. Cervantes, Don Quixote II. 442). NOUN ward n.1, a watchman, guard, keeper, warden (obsolete, OE-1473): OE "Nu scylun hergan hefaen-ricaes uard." (Caedmon, Hymn 1); OE "Weard Scildinga, se þe holmclifu healdan scolde." OED frequency of the verb: about 2 occurrences per million words in modern written English. The OED pages supplied have no quotation of the verb after 1913 and none of the noun after ?1473, so no PDE use is shown here. The OED pages for ward v.2, ward n.2, and the list of compounds and derived words were not supplied, so a warding adjective, a warding gerund and the compound fyrward are not covered.

Fastolf duryng hese noun-age to you and T. H. [etc.]." (J. Russe in Paston Letters & Papers, 2004, II. 104); EMdE 1540 "Personnes, to whom the kinges highnes shall graunt the custodye and wardeship of any of his graces wardes." Blackstone, Commentaries II. v. 67); LMdE 1884 "Sect. 35..assigns to the Chancery Division the wardship of infants." (Law Times 77. 309/1). Sense 1.b, general guardianship, protection, custody, chiefly figurative, 1631-: 1631 "[He] freed this kingdome from the wardship of the Peeres." (J. historical_spelling: wardein, wardeyn, wardayn, wardain, wardane, wardens, warden, wardened
job: the guardian or keeper, used as a title (noun); to watch over as a warden (verb)
definition: Noun: one who guards, protects, or defends; occasionally a guardian angel (OED warden n.1, sense 1.a, obsolete); one who has the care of something specified, a keeper (2.a, obsolete except poetic); and many offices from the guardian of an heir to the head of a college or an air-raid warden. Verb: to watch over or guard as a warden (OED warden v., from 1910).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED warden n.1 and warden v.): NOUN sense 1.a, one who guards, protects, or defends; occasionally a guardian angel (obsolete, ?c1225-1513): ?c1225 "Wat crist ure vchan. to swa gentil wardein bereð to lute menske." (Ancrene Riwle, MS Cleopatra C.vi, 232); c1290 "Þere in seint Iohanes warde is swete moder he tok,..hire wardein he was aftur also þat he to heouene i-wende." (John 31 in S.E. Leg. 403); c1400 "There is none so caitif pilgrym that he ne hath assigned hym a wardeyne the hour of his byrthe." (Pylgr. Sowle i. vii.). Sense 2.a, one who has the care of something specified; a keeper (obsolete except poetic, a1290-): a1290 "Þe hayward nom and bleu his horn, For he wes wardein of þat corn." (S. Eustace 230); 1362 "For Rihtfoliche Resoun schulde rulen ou alle, And kuynde wit be wardeyn oure weolþe to kepe." (W. G. Rossetti, Eden Bower, Poems xxi). Sense 3, guardian of the person and lands of an orphan heir (obsolete, c1290-1700): 1385 "Thus here wardeynys wolde they disceyue." (G. Chaucer, Legend of Good Women 753); 1579 "Wardeine most properly is he that hath the wardship or keeping of an heire" (Rastell, Exposition Termes of Lawes 97b). Sense 4.a, regent or viceroy (obsolete except historical, a1400-); 4.b, governor of a town, province or district, Warden of the Marches (1297-1917): 1470-85 "And sire Brastias was maade wardeyn to wayte vpon the northe fro Trent forwardes." (T. Malory, Morte d'Arthur i. viii. 44). Sense 5, a guild officer, 1389-: 1640 "Next year wee will haue him warden Of our societie." (P. Massinger, Parliament of Love iv. ii. 57). Sense 6.a, the person having the direction or oversight of some work or enterprise (obsolete, 1398-1601): 1601 "Pythagoras, a great maister and warden of these exercises." (P. Holland, trans. Pliny). Sense 2.d, a gatekeeper, porter, sentinel, now rare, a1250-: 1801 "Fit warden of the sorcery-gate" (R. Southey, Thalaba II. xii. 314); 1894 "Female wardens made a fit outpost for this palace of many women." (R. L. Stevenson, In the South Seas iv. iii. 319). Sense 8.a, custodian of a building, esp. a temple or church (obsolete, 1290-1642): 1642 "The good Herald..is a Warden of the temple of Honour." (T. Fuller, Holy State ii. xxii. 141). Sense 11, head of a college, school or hospital, 1575-: 1855 "..a fitting residence for a warden." (A. Trollope, The Warden i. 3). Sense 12, prison keeper, c1330-: 1330 "Wiþ wardeyns þat hem vndertoke." (R. Mannyng, Chronicle Wace 13112). Sense 7.c, an air-raid warden, 1936-: 1936 "An organization of 'air raid wardens' to give immediate information and to help in dealing with fires caused by incendiary bombs." (Times 11 July 16/4); latest noun quotation 1978 "A tin-hatted Air Raid Warden was hurrying along the street... The Warden hurried on." (E. Malpass, Wind brings up Rain xxvi. 232). (T. Hardy, The Dynasts ii. i. vi. 165); 1971 "Having wardened at the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds reserve at Loch Garten, may I enlarge upon the letter from M. S. M. Burns?" (Times 7 May 17/7); 1974 "It would be wardened and visited regularly to prevent vandalism and litter." (Oxford Times 4 January 7/6); 1982 "The eyres are well wardened against egg collectors."
